text:
B: Hiya. Can you hear me okay?
A: Yes. Hello. I'm Tomasz.
B: Lorraine. I'm near Wrexham. Have you had a busy day?
A: Erm, not too bad. I was on shift last night, so I'm a bit slow. Sorry if I'm slow.
B: Oh, don't be daft. What do you do?
A: Packing line, food factory. And I'm a student, archaeology, at Exeter. Second year.
B: Oh, I thought you looked like a student, with the books. You reminded me of my son, actually. Sorry, that sounds awful.
A: No, it's fine. I'm thirty-seven, I'm not offended to look young.
B: Thirty-seven and doing a degree, good for you. I couldn't. I'd be terrified.
A: I was terrified. I'm still, sometimes. Everyone is nineteen.
B: Well. I don't know if that's... sorry, go on.
A: No, it's alright. What do you do?
B: Nothing at the minute. I ran the cleaning team at the college, mornings, then took redundancy. Looking for something part-time. It's knocked me a bit, if I'm honest, starting again at my age.
A: Mm. Yeah. I know this feeling.
B: You do, don't you, with the uni.
A: My wife is pharmacist at the hospital. When I saw your picture I thought you look like the ladies she works with. The nice ones. That's a compliment.
B: Oh, thanks, love. I'll take that.
A: Wrexham, erm. Isn't Offa's Dyke near you?
B: It is, yes. It goes past Ruabon, not far. I've walked bits of it. It's just a big bank, really, isn't it.
A: Just a big bank, yes, but think about it. Eighth century, a king in Mercia decides to dig a line from nearly one sea to the other, by hand, with no machines. Thousands of people, shovels, baskets. And there's another one near you, Wat's Dyke, older maybe, and people still argue about who built which and why. So when you walk on it you're standing on something somebody was told to build twelve hundred years ago. I find that... I don't know. Amazing. Sorry. I talk too much about dirt.
B: No, I didn't know any of that. I'll look at it different now.
A: Do you walk a lot?
B: Most days. Ponciau Banks, round the lanes. That's all old coal tips, the Banks. My grandad was at Hafod colliery.
A: Really? That's archaeology too. Industrial. Somebody will dig your grandad's pit one day and write an essay.
B: Oh, he'd laugh at that. He'd say they want their heads looking at.
A: Probably they do.
B: Do you get home much? You said, Poland, was it?
A: Lublin. Once or twice a year. I ring my mum every Sunday.
B: That's nice. You keep doing that. I lost my mam three years ago, and I still pick the phone up sometimes to ring her. Silly, isn't it.
A: No. It's not silly.
B: I don't know why I said that. Sorry.
A: It's fine. Really. What did she —
